word_bank.example: The coach used periodisation to divide the season into phases — each one building on the last.
Elite marathon runners typically have a very high VO2 max, allowing them to use oxygen extremely efficiently.
Training just below the lactate threshold teaches the body to clear lactic acid more efficiently.
The sports scientist used biomechanics analysis to correct the sprinter's running posture.
Resistance training with moderate weight and high volume is the most effective method for hypertrophy.
After four weeks of intense training, the coach scheduled a deload week to prevent burnout.
Balance board exercises improve proprioception, helping athletes know where their body is in space.
Ignoring rest days and always pushing harder can lead to overtraining, which actually reduces performance.
The entire training programme was designed to bring the athlete to peak performance on the day of the championship.
The body's adaptation to regular training means you must keep increasing the challenge to continue improving.

stage_2_story.text_en:
Moshe's grandson Daniel is in his second year studying sports science at the university in Tel Aviv. Last Friday evening, the whole family came for Shabbat dinner, and Daniel arrived carrying a thick folder of notes under his arm.

'Grandpa,' Daniel said, settling into the chair opposite Moshe, 'I am writing my paper on elite athletic preparation. Can I explain it to you? I need to practise talking about it simply.'

Moshe raised an eyebrow. 'You want to explain university science to a retired plumber? Go ahead, motek. I am listening.'

Daniel laughed. 'OK. Everything in elite sport is built around periodisation — dividing the training year into specific phases. You do not train the same way in January as you do the week before a championship. Each phase has a purpose.'

Moshe nodded slowly. 'So it is like building a house. First the foundations, then the walls, then the roof.'

'Exactly!' Daniel said. 'In the first phase, athletes work on conditioning and biomechanics — how the body moves — to build an efficient base. Then they work on raising their VO2 max and lactate threshold, which determines how hard they can push before their muscles stop cooperating.'

'And what is that word — hypertrophy?' Moshe asked, squinting at Daniel's notes.

'That is when muscles grow bigger and stronger through resistance training. But if you train too hard without rest, you get overtraining — which is the enemy of improvement. So coaches plan deload weeks where everything gets lighter. And throughout it all, they work on proprioception — the body's ability to know where it is in space, which prevents injury.'

Moshe sat quietly for a moment. Then he said: 'So the whole point is adaptation — teaching the body to handle more and more, until the athlete reaches peak performance at exactly the right moment.'

Daniel stared at him. 'Grandpa… that is literally the conclusion of my paper.'

Moshe winked and reached for another piece of challah. 'I told you — sixty years of laying pipes teaches you something about systems.'
